sources.title: 5 Easy Ways to Get Rid of Aquarium Pest Snails (Aquarium Co-Op)
Dipping Plants to Eliminate Snails (That Pet Place)
Aquarium Pest Identification Guide: Snails, Worms and Hydra (Gensou)
Ốc Hại Trong Bể Thủy Sinh: Nguyên Nhân, Tác Hại và Cách Xử Lý (Zen Aquarius)
Cách xử lý ốc hại trong bể thủy sinh (Thái Hòa Aquarium)
Aquarium Snails: What to Keep and What to Avoid (Chewy)

facts.fact: The snails usually called pests in aquariums are bladder, ramshorn and Malaysian trumpet snails (MTS).
These snails eat algae, leftover food, fish waste and dead or sickly plant matter. Aquarium Co-Op says they do not harm live fish or healthy plants.
Gensou says bladder, ramshorn and MTS do not harm healthy plants or fish. The trouble comes from their numbers growing too large.
Zen Aquarius says that when ramshorn snails get too numerous they eat young leaves, especially on weak or soft plants.
Zen Aquarius says Melanoides tuberculata burrows and churns the substrate. When the snails are very numerous they can make the substrate mushy and spoil the aquascape.
Zen Aquarius says bladder snails do not directly harm plants. They spoil the look of the tank and lower water quality through fast breeding and the waste they build up.
Bladder snails (Physella acuta) have thin, translucent shells.
Ramshorn snails have flat, coiled shells that are brown, red or pink.
Zen Aquarius describes ramshorn snails as about 1-2 cm across.
Malaysian trumpet snails have cone- or trumpet-shaped shells. They are nocturnal and stay buried in the gravel.
MTS burrow into the substrate by day and come out at night, so they often go unnoticed until their numbers surge.
Bladder and ramshorn snails lay egg sacs holding many young. MTS give birth to live young and leave no egg clutches.
Assassin snails (Anentome helena) are about 1 inch (2.5 cm) long and eat other snails. They are useful snails and should not be mistaken for pests.
Chewy describes assassin snails as striped like a bumblebee.
Pest snails and their eggs most often arrive on live aquatic plants.
Snails can also arrive in the water at the bottom of a fish bag from the store.
Excess food, fish waste, algae, dying plant matter and mulm feed snail populations.
Overfeeding is the main driver of snail population booms.
Chewy says overfeeding, excess algae from too much light or food, and too little plant growth or too much fertilizer can keep snail populations going.
Snail eggs can come in on stones, sand, plants or substrate, or with water added to the tank.
A single bladder snail can start an infestation because it is a hermaphrodite and can lay viable eggs alone.
A few bladder snails arriving on one plant can become hundreds within weeks.
First, cut feeding to what the fish finish in a few minutes.
Prune plants regularly, scrub algae and vacuum the gravel to remove mulm and debris that feed snails.
Pick snails out by hand or with planting tweezers, and siphon small snails into a bucket during water changes.
Hand removal works less well against MTS because they stay buried in the substrate.
Use a snail trap baited with vegetables or fish food. Traps help catch burrowing, nocturnal snails like MTS.
Leave a piece of cucumber or carrot in the tank overnight, then lift it out the next morning with the snails on it. This has to be repeated many times.
A fresh lettuce leaf left in a corner overnight can be removed with the snails in the morning. This controls snails but does not remove 100% of them.
Blanched zucchini in a submerged bottle can be used as a home-made snail trap.
Snail-eating fish include pufferfish from pea puffer to Mbu puffer, and clown, zebra, yoyo and dwarf chain loaches.
Chewy advises against clown loaches as snail control because of their large size and need to school. It suggests smaller loaches such as Yasuhikotakia sidthimunki.
Snail-eating fish only work well against small snails and baby snails. The species must suit the tank size.
Assassin snails (Anentome helena) eat other snails, including larger ones.

Rachel O'Leary, quoted by Chewy, advises keeping assassin snails in a small bare tank rather than a display tank. Their eggs spread easily on plants, wood, rocks or sponge filters, and released snails could become invasive.
Copper sulfate: the 96-hour LC50 for pond snails at 20 °C is 0.39 mg/L. A typical aquarium treatment should stay at 0.15–0.2 ppm.
Do not double a copper dose, because toxicity does not rise in a straight line with dose.
Copper toxicity rises with temperature. The author suggests treating at about 22–23 °C.
Hard, alkaline water binds copper and makes it less effective. In soft, acidic water, start at about half the copper dose.
During copper treatment, take the filter out and keep it alive in a bucket of water to protect the nitrifying bacteria. Keep strong aeration going.
Copper does not kill snail eggs. A repeat treatment within about two weeks may be needed for newly hatched snails.
Shrimp, crabs and other invertebrates are highly sensitive to copper. Do not use copper sulfate when they are in the tank.
Vallisneria and Sagittaria are sensitive to copper. Anubias and most mosses generally survive the recommended doses.
Too much copper can cause red sores on the sides of fish.
Copper cannot break down and leaves the tank only through water changes. Activated carbon removes some of it, and a water conditioner with chelating agents can inactivate what remains.
Copper-based snail killers kill invertebrates and some plants.
Aquarium Co-Op advises against bleach or aquarium salt for snails. A dose that kills snails and eggs without harming sensitive plants like vallisneria and cryptocoryne is hard to find.
Zen Aquarius notes that snail killers such as copper sulfate and Snailaway work fast but can affect fish and plants, and ornamental shrimp are especially sensitive.
Plant dip, alum: 1-3 tablespoons per gallon of warm water, for at least 2-3 hours for stronger solutions or up to 24 hours for milder ones. Alum kills snails but works less well on eggs.
Plant dip, alum: 2-3 teaspoons per quart of water for 2-3 days. It can harm plants.

Plant dip, bleach: use plain liquid chlorine bleach at no more than 1 part to 19 parts water (just over ¾ cup per gallon). Dip for no more than 2 minutes for sensitive plants or 3 minutes for hardier ones.
Plant dip, bleach: Chewy gives 1 part bleach to 20 parts water, followed by thorough rinsing.
Plant dip, potassium permanganate: mix with warm water to a dark pink solution and soak for 10-20 minutes. Then rinse in dechlorinated water.
Plant dip, salt: 1 cup of aquarium or kosher salt per gallon. Swish the plant for about 15-20 seconds, keeping the roots above the water. Do not use table or iodized salt.
Never mix potassium permanganate with hydrogen peroxide, formalin, formaldehyde or anything containing alcohol, because they form a noxious gas.
When snails die en masse after a treatment, remove the dead snails promptly and do a large water change of about 50%. Decaying snails release ammonia that can harm fish more than the copper does.
Check new plants and remove every snail and egg by hand, rinse them under running water, then grow them in a lit, fertilized quarantine tank and keep removing any snails that appear.
Snail eggs take 1–4 weeks to hatch, depending on species and temperature. Plant quarantine is not foolproof.
Always dip plants in a separate bucket or tub, never in the aquarium. Test the dip on one plant first, and rinse in dechlorinated water before planting.
Wash and disinfect new plants, and never add water from the fish store to your tank.
Change water and clean the tank regularly, and feed only what the fish eat within a few minutes.
Using copper coins or wire against snails does not work: metallic copper does not release usable ions and can bring in pathogens.
Using copper snail killers while snail numbers are still high is a mistake. Use them only after the population is under control, because the dead snails foul the water.
Leaving killed snails to rot in the tank is a mistake. Feed them to snail-eating fish instead, or crush them.
Throwing out used gravel briefly is not enough to get rid of MTS: they can survive in dry, used gravel for many months.
Myth: one snail cannot breed. Aquarium Co-Op says bladder snails can reproduce alone and lay viable eggs.
Myth: 'pest' snails harm plants and fish. Aquarium Co-Op and Gensou say they do not harm healthy plants or fish and are part of the tank's ecosystem.
Vietnamese guides call these snails 'ốc hại'. Zen Aquarius calls Melanoides tuberculata 'ốc viền đỏ' and the bladder snail 'ốc bàng quang'.
Thái Hòa Aquarium names the pest snails 'ốc xoắn' and 'ốc đỉa'. It recommends cá lóc (snakehead) and cá chuột Mỹ (corydoras) as snail eaters, plus ốc Helena (assassin snail).
Zen Aquarius lists snail-eating fish used in Vietnam as cá chuột, loach, cá bảy màu (guppy) and puffer.
Vietnamese shops mention copper sulfate and Snailaway as snail killers but give no doses. They advise reading the product label carefully.
Chewy says apple snails (in Vietnam, ốc bươu vàng and relatives) and other pond snails should be kept out of home aquariums.
Copper sulfate also works as an algaecide, antibacterial, antifungal and treatment for ich.
